author: sleepinyourhat
text: That'd be a weird, uncomfortable situation for us to be in. And it's really hard to figure out whether it *is* the situation we're in. So, uh, I guess I'm glad there are people working on philosophy of mind?

author: sleepinyourhat
text: But that'd be because of the properties of the actual systems we have now, not because of some deep fact about the universe.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So even on this view, we'd be justified in saying that in real moral tradeoffs between impacts on humans (or most social animals) and impacts on artificial systems, humans (etc.) always win.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The good news is that current NNs don't very closely resemble anything that we'd confidently recognize as phenomenally conscious, and they're many orders of magnitude less complex and less numerous.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: And that question of *how much* is would even be morally relevant! If something has experiences (marginally, sorta), it probably deserves some moral consideration (marginally, sorta).

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So, sure, it's plausible that a language model is 'slightly' conscious. But so is a thermostat. Or a compost pile. Figuring out *how much* is the hard part.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I think that's fairly intuitive! Without that, it's really hard to see how we'd identify a sharp line delimiting what's phenomenally conscious and what's not.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: On that view, basically every system of any kind is very very 'slightly' phenomenally conscious. Even if it doesn't have any kind of self-awareness, it has 'experiences' to some (potentially extremely limited) degree.
